title: THE BIBLE NEVER CALLED HER A PROSTITUTE. SO WHY HAVE WE BEEN CALLING HER ONE FOR CENTURIES?
paragraphs: THE BIBLE NEVER CALLED HER A PROSTITUTE. SO WHY HAVE WE BEEN CALLING HER ONE FOR CENTURIES?

Jesus knew about her five husbands. He knew about the man she was living with. But what happened at that well was not the public humiliation of an immoral woman. It was a divine encounter that exposes how easily religious people can confuse someone's painful history with their identity—and how radically Jesus sees the people we have already judged.
There is something deeply disturbing about the way we have told her story.

For generations, she has stood in sermons, Bible studies, Christian books, and church conversations as the woman with five husbands. The immoral woman. The promiscuous woman. The woman who supposedly went from man to man because she could not control her desires.
Some have even called her a prostitute.
And perhaps you have heard that description so many times that you assumed it was written somewhere in your Bible.
But open John chapter 4.
Read it carefully.
Read what Jesus actually said.
Then read what He did not say.
Because there is one word that generations of people have attached to this woman that the Gospel of John never uses.
Prostitute.
Not once.
And that absence matters more than we might realize.
Not because sexual sin is unimportant. Not because repentance is optional. Not because Jesus overlooks the truth about our lives.
But because the Savior who knows everything about a person does not give us permission to invent what Scripture has not revealed.
And somewhere in this story is a person who has spent years carrying a name that God never gave them.
Maybe that person is you.
The encounter begins with a tired Jesus sitting beside Jacob's well near the Samaritan town of Sychar.
John tells us that it was about the sixth hour. On the usual Jewish reckoning, that would place the encounter around noon.
Jesus was weary from His journey.
That detail alone is astonishing.
The eternal Word who became flesh, the One through whom all things were made, was genuinely tired.
He sat beside a well.
And a Samaritan woman came to draw water.
Jesus asked her for a drink.
That sounds ordinary until we understand the world surrounding the conversation.
Jews and Samaritans had a long history of religious and ethnic hostility. Their disagreements involved ancestry, sacred history, worship, and the proper place to approach God.
And in that culture, a Jewish man initiating this kind of conversation with an unfamiliar Samaritan woman was unusual enough that even His disciples would later marvel.
Yet Jesus spoke first.
Not with an accusation.
Not with a warning.
Not with a lecture about her reputation.
He asked for water.
Sometimes the most extraordinary moments of grace begin with something painfully ordinary.
A conversation.
A question.
An unexpected kindness from someone who had every social reason to walk away.
The woman was surprised.
John 4:9 records her asking why a Jewish man would request a drink from a Samaritan woman.
But Jesus had come for more than water.
He began speaking about the gift of God and the living water He could give.
In the Greek text of John 4:10, the expression is ὕδωρ ζῶν (hydōr zōn)—literally, "living water."
In ordinary usage, living water could describe fresh, flowing water rather than stagnant water.
But Jesus was drawing her toward something far greater than a better source of drinking water.
He was speaking of the life God gives, a reality John later connects with the Holy Spirit in John 7:37–39.
The woman initially understood Him in terms of physical water.
She saw a deep well.
She saw a man without a bucket.
She saw an impossible offer.
But Jesus saw a thirst that no earthly well could satisfy.
He told her that ordinary water would leave a person thirsty again, but the water He gives would become a spring welling up to eternal life.
Imagine hearing that promise while carrying a life full of unanswered questions.
Imagine standing before someone who speaks as though the emptiness you have learned to live with does not have to be permanent.
She asked Him for that water.
And then the conversation took a turn that has been misunderstood by countless readers.
Jesus said:
"Go, call thy husband, and come hither." — John 4:16, KJV
She answered:
"I have no husband." — John 4:17, KJV
Jesus responded:
"Thou hast well said, I have no husband: For thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband: in that saidst thou truly." — John 4:17–18, KJV
And there it is.
The passage that has become the foundation for so many assumptions about this woman.
Five husbands.
A sixth man who was not her husband.
And suddenly, in the imagination of many readers, an entire biography appears.
She must have been sexually reckless.
She must have seduced men.
She must have destroyed marriages.
She must have been a prostitute.
But stop.
Where does the passage actually say those things?
It doesn't.
The Greek of John 4:18 includes these words:
πέντε γὰρ ἄνδρας ἔσχες (pente gar andras esches)
"For you have had five husbands."
The word ἄνδρας (andras) can mean men or husbands depending on context. Here, the surrounding conversation clearly concerns husbands.
Jesus then says:
καὶ νῦν ὃν ἔχεις οὐκ ἔστιν σου ἀνήρ (kai nyn hon echeis ouk estin sou anēr)
"And the one you now have is not your husband."
Notice what Jesus reveals.
He knows her marital history.
He knows her present relationship does not constitute a marriage.
He knows she has spoken truthfully about having no husband.
But He does not explain why those five marriages ended.
He does not say whether she was widowed.
He does not say whether she was divorced.
He does not tell us whether she was abandoned, mistreated, or responsible for the breakdown of any of those relationships.
He does not identify the nature of her present arrangement beyond saying that the man she now has is not her husband.
Those missing details are not invitations for us to manufacture certainty.
They are boundaries around what we can responsibly claim.
In the ancient world, women could be profoundly vulnerable to decisions made by men.
Widowhood could bring financial insecurity.
Divorce could leave a woman socially and economically exposed.
A woman might have endured repeated losses or rejection with very little power to determine what happened next.
Does that prove the Samaritan woman was an innocent victim of five tragedies?
No.
And we must be just as careful not to invent a tragic biography as we are not to invent a scandalous one.
The truth is that Scripture does not tell us why she had five husbands.
We simply do not know.
And that is precisely the point.
There is a difference between recognizing a morally complicated situation and claiming to know every motive, action, and failure that produced it.
Jesus knew.
We don't.
Yet sometimes we speak as though we were standing beside that well with a complete record of her private life.
There is another detail that deserves attention.
John never uses the Greek word πόρνη (pornē)—a word meaning prostitute—to describe this woman.
Nor does he explicitly accuse her of adultery.
That does not mean her present relationship was necessarily righteous. Jesus plainly identifies a distinction between the man she has and a husband.
The passage is not a declaration that every relationship is acceptable.
But neither is it evidence that she sold sex or habitually pursued men.
Those are different claims.
And biblical faithfulness requires us to keep them different.
Why does this matter?
Because we can become so comfortable condemning sins that we begin condemning people for sins we cannot even establish.
We turn suspicion into certainty.
We turn speculation into doctrine.
We turn someone's incomplete story into a public warning.
And then we call it discernment.
But discernment is not the ability to imagine the worst about someone.
It is the responsibility to judge truthfully, humbly, and according to what God has actually revealed.
Jesus Himself said in John 7:24:
"Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment."
That command does not prohibit moral judgment.
It demands that our judgment be righteous.
And righteous judgment cannot be built on invented evidence.
Perhaps this is where the story begins to hurt.
Because some people reading this know what it feels like to have others tell a version of their lives that leaves out the truth.
They know what it is to be reduced to a divorce.
A pregnancy.
A failed relationship.
A broken family.
A past addiction.
A public mistake.
A season of rebellion.
Something they did.
Something done to them.
Or something people simply assumed.
They know what it feels like to enter a room and wonder whether everyone already believes a story they never had the chance to explain.
And the painful thing is that sometimes the harshest voices belong to people who know the language of grace but have forgotten how to practice it.
Yet this passage is not merely a warning against judgmental religion.
It is a revelation of Jesus Christ.
Watch what happens after Jesus exposes His knowledge of the woman's life.
She says:
"Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet." — John 4:19, KJV
Then she raises the dispute between Samaritan and Jewish worship.
Some readers treat this as an obvious attempt to change the subject.
Perhaps it was.
But John does not tell us her motive.
She may also have been responding to the discovery that she was speaking with someone who possessed prophetic knowledge.
What matters is how Jesus responds.
He does not refuse to discuss theology with her.
He does not say that her personal history makes her unworthy of spiritual understanding.
He engages her question about worship.
And then He reveals something that reaches far beyond her individual circumstances.
In John 4:23, Jesus declares that true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth.
The Greek expression is:
ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ (en pneumati kai alētheia)
"In spirit and truth."
Not merely at the correct mountain.
Not merely through inherited religious arguments.
But through the worship made possible by God's saving work, in accordance with His truth.
Jesus is not offering spirituality without repentance or worship without obedience.
He is announcing the coming reality of worship centered on the revelation and saving work of the Messiah.
And then the woman speaks of the Messiah who is coming.
Jesus answers in John 4:26:
"Ἐγώ εἰμι, ὁ λαλῶν σοι."
"I am he, the one speaking to you."

The Greek words ἐγώ εἰμι (egō eimi) mean "I am." In this sentence, Jesus is directly identifying Himself as the Messiah she expects. John's Gospel also uses this expression in other passages with profound theological significance.
Consider the wonder of that moment.
A Samaritan woman stands beside a well.
She has a history Jesus knows in full.
She belongs to a community divided from the Jews by generations of hostility.
And Jesus openly identifies Himself to her as the promised Messiah.
Not because her history is irrelevant.
Not because truth no longer matters.
But because God's saving grace reaches people whose lives are far more complicated than religious labels can explain.
This is what makes the Gospel so astonishing.
Jesus does not need to falsify our innocence in order to offer us mercy.
And He does not need to exaggerate our guilt in order to demonstrate His holiness.
He already knows the truth.
All of it.
The things others misunderstood.
The things we have concealed.
The wounds we did not cause.
The wrongs we did commit.
The sins we have tried to justify.
The regrets that still visit us in the quiet.
He sees without distortion.
And His call is not to remain hidden but to come into the light.
There is another popular claim about this woman that deserves examination.
People often say she came to the well at noon because the other women rejected her and she wanted to avoid their judgment.
It is possible.
But John never explicitly says that.
The unusual hour may invite questions, but it does not establish her social reputation.
We should not present an imaginative reconstruction as though it were a recorded fact.
And when we move from what Scripture says to what Scripture might allow, humility should govern our language.
That humility makes the actual story even more beautiful.
Because we do not need to invent a hostile village to appreciate the miracle that follows.
John tells us that the woman left her water jar and went into the town.
She began speaking to the people.
"Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" — John 4:29, KJV
Read that again.
Come, see.
She does not deliver a polished sermon.
She does not claim to understand every mystery of the faith.
She does not pretend that her life has always been righteous.
She points people toward Jesus.
And notice the way she speaks about His knowledge of her.
She does not say, "Come see the man who humiliated me."
She does not say, "Come see the man who publicly destroyed my reputation."
She tells them about someone who knew her life.
Her words are a personal testimony, not a transcript of every event that ever happened to her.
And that testimony mattered.
John 4:39 says:
"And many of the Samaritans of that city believed on him for the saying of the woman, which testified, He told me all that ever I did."
Many believed because of her testimony.
Then others came to Jesus, heard Him for themselves, and confessed that He was indeed the Savior of the world.
The woman was not the Savior.
Her testimony was not the foundation of salvation.
Jesus was.
And that is what makes her witness powerful.
A person does not have to possess a spotless history to tell the truth about a spotless Savior.
But there is something else we must not miss.
The Gospel of John does not explicitly record this woman's later life.
It does not give us a detailed account of her repentance, her subsequent relationships, or how she lived in the years that followed.
We should not manufacture those details either.
Her encounter with Jesus and her witness to the town are enough to show what John wants us to see.
Christ crossed barriers.
Christ revealed truth.
Christ offered living water.
Christ disclosed His identity.
And people came to believe in Him.
This is not a story about how the world was wrong to call a woman sinful because she was secretly perfect.
It is a story about how the world's categories are too small to contain the mercy, knowledge, and saving purpose of Jesus Christ.
And it forces us to ask an uncomfortable question.
How many people have we stopped listening to because we thought we already knew their story?
How many have we treated as permanently disqualified because of something in their past?
How many times have we been more interested in discovering someone's scandal than in helping them encounter the Savior?
And how many times have we used the truth of God's holiness as an excuse for our own cruelty?
We must not swing to the opposite extreme.
The Gospel is not permission to excuse sin.
Jesus never taught that repentance was unnecessary.
He began His public ministry announcing the kingdom of God and calling people to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15).
He warned people against remaining in sin.
He taught that evil comes from the human heart.
He called sinners to follow Him.
And at the cross, He bore the judgment our sins deserve.
Grace is not God pretending evil does not matter.
Grace is God acting in Christ to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
Not while we were already impressive.
Not after we had repaired our reputations.
Not after we had earned the right to be loved.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and new life are offered to all who turn to Him in faith.
That is the heart of this story.
Not the five husbands.
Not the mystery of the sixth man.
Not the scandal we have imagined.
Jesus.
The One who sat beside the well.
The One who knew the truth.
The One who offered living water.
The One who revealed Himself as Messiah.
The One who would eventually go to the cross and rise from the grave.
The One who still calls thirsty souls to Himself.
And perhaps the most searching question in this passage is not what kind of woman she was.
Perhaps it is what kind of people we become when we read about her.
Do we become more careful with the truth?
More compassionate toward the wounded?
More serious about sin without becoming reckless with accusations?
More eager to introduce people to Christ than to expose them to public contempt?
Or do we read the passage, identify someone else's supposed failures, and walk away feeling superior?
The woman at the well is not an invitation to celebrate moral confusion.
She is not an excuse to erase biblical standards.
But neither is she a blank page on which we may write every sexual accusation we can imagine.
She is a real person in the Gospel narrative.
And Jesus treated her as someone worthy of a serious conversation about eternal life.
That should change the way we speak about people.
It should change the way we preach.
It should change the way we respond when someone confesses a complicated past.
It should even change the way we tell our own stories.
Because some of us have spent so long identifying ourselves by our worst chapter that we have forgotten the Gospel announces a new identity in Christ.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
That promise does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It does not mean all broken relationships are automatically repaired.
It does not mean repentance is painless or that healing happens overnight.
It means that union with Jesus Christ brings a genuinely new life.
The past is no longer the final authority over the believer's identity.
Christ is.
And perhaps that is why this encounter has endured for nearly two thousand years.
Because every generation contains people who are thirsty.
Some are thirsty beneath religious appearances.
Some are thirsty beneath achievements and applause.
Some are thirsty after years of destructive choices.
Some are thirsty because others wounded them.
Some are thirsty while sitting in church every Sunday, singing songs about grace but secretly wondering whether grace could ever reach the truth about their lives.
And Jesus still speaks about living water.
He still tells the truth.
He still calls people to believe.
He still receives sinners who come to Him.
He still transforms lives through the Gospel.
You may have been called a failure.
A disgrace.
A hypocrite.
Unworthy.
Too far gone.
Perhaps some of those words came from people who should have helped you find your way back to God.
But listen carefully.
The answer is not to declare yourself innocent of everything.
The answer is to bring your entire life before the Savior who knows the difference between what happened to you and what you have done.
Confess what is truly sin.
Refuse to carry guilt for accusations that are not true.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Receive the mercy offered through Jesus Christ.
And begin walking in the truth.
You do not have to defend every chapter of your past to come to Jesus.
But you do have to come to Him.
Not merely to admire His kindness.
Not merely to find relief from shame.
But to trust Him as Savior and follow Him as Lord.
That is where grace leads.
Not into hiding.
Into the light.
And there is something extraordinary about what happened in Samaria.
The woman's invitation was simple.
"Come, see."
She pointed beyond herself.
And others encountered Christ.
That is still the calling of every faithful Christian witness.
Not to build our own fame.
Not to create a following around our personalities.
Not to turn people's wounds into entertainment.
But to make Jesus known.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Because there are people scrolling through their phones right now who have not opened a Bible in years.
People who are silently struggling with sin.
People who have been wounded by careless religion.
People who need sound biblical teaching instead of another shallow motivational message.
People who need to hear that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and Jesus Christ is sufficient.
And sometimes one article, shared at the right moment, becomes the beginning of a conversation that leads someone back to Scripture.
So if this message made you reconsider how you have spoken about someone's past, do not let that conviction disappear when you close this page.
Not to prove that you are more compassionate than someone else.
Not to start another argument.
But because someone in your circle may desperately need to know that Jesus sees them more truthfully than the world does.
And if you have been quietly carrying shame, or if this passage has exposed a judgmental attitude in your own heart, there is room for an honest response.
You do not have to disclose private details to strangers to prove that your response is sincere.
God already knows what is in your heart.
And if you need prayer, you can simply say, "Pray for me."
We want Gospel Warrior to be more than a place where people briefly feel inspired.
We want it to be a place where believers are continually drawn back to Scripture, challenged to repent, encouraged to persevere, and reminded that Jesus Christ is the center of everything.
There is also a deeper way to help this mission continue.
It is not a requirement for faithful Christian living.
And it is not a replacement for supporting your local church or fulfilling the responsibilities of Christian generosity.
Biblically, giving must never be presented as a way to purchase forgiveness, spiritual blessing, or salvation.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds believers that giving should be voluntary and cheerful, not forced by pressure or guilt.
But supporting trustworthy Gospel ministry can be a meaningful expression of Christian generosity.
They are simply a way of expressing appreciation to those who help sustain the work.
The deeper reason is the mission.
More Scripture.
More faithful teaching.
More encouragement for struggling believers.
More opportunities to point people away from despair and toward Jesus Christ.
Pray for it.
Share the Gospel.
Invite someone to read the Scriptures for themselves.
Help someone who has been wounded by condemnation discover the difference between human accusation and the conviction of the Holy Spirit.
Because genuine conviction leads us toward repentance and Christ.
Cruel condemnation often leaves people staring only at themselves.
And the world does not need another generation of Christians who know how to expose a scandal but have forgotten how to proclaim redemption.
It needs believers who love truth enough not to distort it.
Who love holiness enough to practice it.
Who love people enough to speak honestly.
And who love Jesus enough to make Him—not human failure—the center of the story.
The Samaritan woman came to a well for water.
She encountered the Messiah.
She went into her town and pointed others toward Him.
And many came to believe.
We do not know everything about her past.
We do not know everything about her future.
But we know whom she met.
And that is the part of her story John wants us to remember.
So the next time someone calls her a prostitute, open the Bible.
Ask where the text says that.
Then keep reading.
Read about the living water.
Read about worship in spirit and truth.
Read about the Messiah who revealed Himself.
Read about the townspeople who believed.
Read until the center of the story is no longer a woman's alleged scandal but the glory of Jesus Christ.
And when you close your Bible, remember that the same Savior who knew the truth about that woman knows the truth about you.
He knows the things you regret.
He knows the things others falsely believe.
He knows the sins you must confess.
He knows the wounds that still need healing.
He knows the fears you cannot explain.
And He is not asking you to rewrite your history to make yourself acceptable.
He calls you to repent, believe the Gospel, and receive the new life that only He can give.
Because the greatest miracle at Jacob's well was not that Jesus knew about five husbands.
It was that the Messiah stood before a thirsty human being and offered the gift of God.
The world may remember the history it thinks it knows about you. But Jesus knows the whole truth—and His grace can write a future your past could never have promised.
